title: Vehicles & Diggers
strapline: Loading, tipping, racing and rescuing — wheels, ramps and the physics of getting the job done.
intent: Explore forces through play that is really an experiment: pushing, pulling, loading, tipping, and racing cars down ramps of different steepness.
Name vehicles precisely and know their jobs — a cement mixer, a fire engine and a recycling lorry do different work for different people.
Build spatial and positional language on the road itself: under the bridge, behind the garage, between the cones, reversing round the bend.
Connect play vehicles to the real people who drive them — the crew on the bin lorry, the paramedic, the delivery driver we wave to.
Design and build purposeful layouts: roads that join up, garages that fit the lorry, bridges strong enough to cross.
implementation: Offer ramps and guttering at different heights and let the racing begin — then wonder aloud why the steep ramp's car went further.
Use the precise names yourself: excavator, dumper, transporter, tanker — children will out-name you within the week.
Give the diggers a real job with real material — gravel to shift, sand to excavate, a road to clear — machines exist to work.
Narrate position as you play alongside: 'you reversed right under the bridge, then round behind the petrol station'.
Add mark-making into the play: road signs, parking permits, a number plate for every garage space.
Stage a breakdown or a blocked road and let children argue out the rescue plan.
On walks, spot working vehicles and the people in them; back inside, replay what the bin crew actually did.
key_questions: Which ramp will send the car furthest — and why do you think that?
What is this digger's job today, and what will it need?
How could the breakdown truck reach the car if the bridge is blocked?
Who drives this one in real life, and how do they help us?
How many loads will it take to move all that gravel?

impact.text: Children push, pull, load and tip with big purposeful movements, carrying and shifting heavy loads across the layout.
Children test ramps and slopes — steeper means faster, further — and compare the runs to find the winner.
Children use positional language on the move — under the bridge, behind the garage, next to the cones, reversing between the lorries.
Children sort the fleet by their own rules — all the diggers, all the emergency ones, big wheels and small.
Children name vehicles precisely and match each to its job — the mixer to the building site, the tanker to the petrol station.
Children build roads, bridges and garages with clear purpose and tell you exactly what each part is for.
Children narrate journeys, breakdowns and rescues as they drive, giving each vehicle a voice and a mission.
Children talk about the real people behind the vehicles — the bin crew, the paramedic, the delivery driver — as people who help us.

enhancements: Guttering, planks and blocks for ramps at three different steepnesses — plus chalk to mark where each car stopped.
A gravel-and-sand quarry tray for the excavators, with buckets to fill and a weigh scale for loads.
Masking-tape roads across the floor with junctions, a roundabout and a zebra crossing to obey.
A car wash: soapy water, brushes, sponges and towels for a muddy fleet.
Number plates and numbered parking bays for matching each car to its own space.
Clipboards, hi-vis vests and 'road closed' signs so the roadworks crew can run the site properly.
Large cardboard boxes and split pins for building a vehicle big enough to sit inside.

playing_exploring: Ramp-racing is trial after trial — children adjust the slope, the car, the launch, and run it again.
Real gravel and sand give the diggers genuine resistance to work against, not just carpet.
active_learning: Moving the whole quarry one bucket at a time is proud, persistent work with a visible finish.
Children keep rebuilding the bridge until the transporter can cross without it collapsing.
creating_thinking: Children predict which ramp wins and revise the theory when the results say otherwise.
A blocked road forces a new route — children plan detours and argue the best way round.
